description:
Observationally speaking, the sky only talks through data, and data matters when someone understands it and tells its story, like a dip in starlight that became an exoplanet. I learned this during my observational astrophysics lab at the Asiago Observatory, where I took this picture. 

Far past Neptune there might be a planet no one has seen, and since SPHEREx maps the whole sky again and again, we want to catch it moving between maps and build a tool so anyone can watch the sky change with us.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a free web page that does for SPHEREx what Clyde Tombaugh did when he found Pluto in 1930. It flips between pictures of the same patch of sky so that anything that moves or changes jumps out. You type any RA and Dec, pick a star, or click a spot on the whole-sky map. The page then plays every SPHEREx exposure of that field as a flipbook on one fixed north-up grid, in all six detectors, with Gaia and CatWISE stars overlaid. The images come live from NASA's IRSA archive in about half a minute.

The challenge asks for a way to find moving and changing objects in SPHEREx data, and the page measures what the eye sees. Its measured track puts Barnard's Star at 10.4 arcseconds a year, the same as Gaia. The exposures themselves give a spectrum and a light curve.

This matters because volunteers flipping images found many of the nearest brown dwarfs. Our page lets anyone sweep the sky, test their eye on a fake mover, and report a candidate in one click. It also shows honestly why SPHEREx is unlikely to catch Planet X.
details:
What it does.

In 1930 Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by flipping between two photographs of the same sky. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 colours of infrared light, and SPHEREx Blink lets anyone do Tombaugh's trick with it. You pick a spot on a whole-sky map made from the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube, with 29 well-known objects and the Sun marked for orientation. You can also type an RA and Dec, or search an exoplanet host star by name from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. The page then plays every SPHEREx exposure of a 6 by 6 arcminute field. It can show one image per exposure or one median per sky pass, as a blink or as a difference image, in any of the six detectors. Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 sources are moved to the date of each frame. Every setting lives in the URL, so one link is one view and can be shared.

How it works.

IRSA does not let browsers read its files directly, so for any position the page asks a small relay on our site. The relay finds every DR1 exposure with IRSA's SIA service. It reads each cutout only as far as the image, flag and zodiacal light planes. It maps every pixel through the TAN-SIP header onto one north-up grid, and it takes the wavelength at the target from the detector's WAVE-TAB table. The same steps run in our Python data path with Astropy. We checked the relay against it in all six detectors and got the same wavelength, the same target pixel, and pixel values within about one percent. The five test targets ship as static files in all six detectors, 60 views in all, so they open at once.

What it measures.

SPHEREx sees through a linear variable filter, so each exposure sees a target at its own wavelength. A blink can therefore mix colour with time, and the page separates the two in three ways. A spectrum panel plots the target's light against wavelength, one dot per exposure, which gives the challenge's spectrum on the fly. A switch blinks only the exposures of one colour. A light curve at that colour shows change in time. A measured track gives the motion. It puts Barnard's Star at 10.4 arcseconds a year against 10.4 from Gaia, Epsilon Indi B at 4.6 against 4.7, and WISE 0855 at 8.5 against 8.2. Kapteyn's Star, which is not one of the five targets, comes out at 8.3 against 8.6 through the live relay. RW Aurigae and R Draconis stay at rest, as they should.

Benefits and intended impact.

Volunteers flipping images found many of the nearest brown dwarfs, through projects like Backyard Worlds. SPHEREx Blink brings that to SPHEREx. A volunteer can sweep the sky one field at a time and train their eye on a fake mover of known brightness and speed placed on real frames. When they spot something, one click reports the candidate as a GitHub issue that holds the exact view and the first checks to make. A story section below the tool explains why we blink the sky at three reading levels, for someone new, a student or a scientist. It is written in English, Indonesian and Italian.

Planet X, honestly.

The challenge is named after Planet X, so we checked whether SPHEREx could catch it. Its motion would be easy to see. Its faintness is the problem, because a Planet Nine of the usual size and distance is fainter in the near infrared than one SPHEREx exposure reaches. The page shows this with a calculator and with the fake mover, and it says plainly what the tool can and cannot do.

How it is creative.

We took a hundred-year-old method, the blink comparator, and pointed it at a survey built for spectra rather than motion. The awkward part of SPHEREx, that every exposure sees a different colour, became a feature. The same frames give a movie, a spectrum and a light curve. The whole sky can be explored in the browser with no install, no account and no login.

Factors we considered.

We wanted the numbers to be right before anything else, so every measured motion is checked against Gaia, and the relay is checked against an independent Python path. We kept the page light, with no frameworks, so it loads on a phone or a slow connection. We made sure any position works, not only the presets, because a fixed demo cannot find anything new. Credits, data DOIs and the use of AI are stated on the page and in every code file.

Tools.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks. Aladin Lite for the sky map. A Vercel serverless function for the relay. Python with Astropy, NumPy and SciPy for the data path. GitHub Actions to export the five targets. LaTeX for the release document.
